text.en: If you meet the Buddha on the road, do not cling even to him; lean on no one, and stand free.

Once when Hyakujo delivered some Zen lectures an old man attended them, unseen by the monks. At the end of each talk when the monks left so did he. But one day he remained after they had gone, and Hyakujo asked him: "Who are you?"

The old man replied: "I am not a human being,  but I was a human being when the Kashapa Buddha preached in this world. I was a Zen master and lived on this mountain. At that time one of my students asked me whether or not the enlightened man is subject to the law of causation. I answered him: 'The enlightened man is not subject to the law of causation.' For this answer evidencing a clinging to absoluteness I became a fox for five hundred rebirths, and I am still a fox. Will you save me from this condition with your Zen words and let me get out of a fox's body? Now may I ask you: Is the enlightened man subject to the law of causation?"

Hyakujo said: "The enlightened man is one with the law of causation."

At the words of Hyakujo the old man was enlightened. "I am emancipated," he said, paying homage with a deep bow. "I am no more a fox, but I have to leave my body in my dwelling place behind this mountain. Please perform my funeral as a monk." Then he disappeared.

The next day Hyakujo gave an order through the chief monk to prepare to attend the funeral of a monk. "No one was sick in the infirmary," wondered the monks. "What does our teacher mean?"

After dinner Hyakujo led the monks out and around the mountain. In a cave, with his staff he poked out the corpse of an old fox and then performed the ceremony of cremation.

That evening Hyakujo gave a talk to the monks and told them this story about the law of causation.

Obaku, upon hearing the story, asked Hyakujo: "I understand that a long time ago because a certain person gave a wrong Zen answer he became a fox for five hundred rebirths. Now I want to  ask: If some modern master is asked many questions and he always gives the right answer, what will become of him?"

Hyakujo said: "You come here near me and I will tell you."

Obaku went near Hyakujo and slapped the teacher's face with his hand, for he knew this was the answer his teacher intended to give him.

Hyakujo clapped his hands and laughed at this discernment. "I thought a Persian had a red beard," he said, "and now I know a Persian who has a red beard."

author: Hyakujo
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 2 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Gutei raised his finger whenever he was asked a question about Zen. A boy attendant began to imitate him in this way. When anyone asked the boy what his master had preached about, the boy would raise his finger.

Gutei heard about the boy's mischief. He seized  him and cut off his finger. The boy cried and ran away. Gutei called and stopped him. When the boy turned his head to Gutei, Gutei raised up his own finger. In that instant the boy was enlightened.

When Gutei was about to pass from this world he gathered his monks around him. "I attained my finger-Zen," he said, "from my teacher Tenryu, and in my whole life I could not exhaust it." Then he passed away.

author: Gutei
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 3 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Wakuan complained when he saw a picture of bearded Bodhidharma: "Why hasn't that fellow a beard?"

author: Wakuan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 4 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Kyogen said: "Zen is like a man hanging in a tree by his teeth over a precipice. His hands grasp no branch, his feet rest on no limb, and under the tree another person asks him: 'Why did Bodhidharma come to China from India?'

"If the man in the tree does not answer, he fails; and if he does answer, he falls and loses his life. Now what shall he do?"

author: Kyogen
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 5 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
When Buddha was in Grdhrakuta mountain he turned a flower in his fingers and held it before his listeners. Every one was silent. Only Maha-Kashapa smiled at this revelation, although he tried to control the lines of his face.

Buddha said: "I have the eye of the true teaching, the heart of Nirvana, the true aspect of non-form, and the ineffable stride of Dharma. It is not expressed by words, but especially transmitted beyond teaching. This teaching I have given to Maha-Kashapa."

author: Maha-Kashapa
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 6 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A monk told Joshu: "I have just entered the monastery. Please teach me."

Joshu asked: "Have you eaten your rice porridge?"

The monk replied: "I have eaten."

Joshu said: "Then you had better wash your bowl."

At that moment the monk was enlightened.

author: Joshu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 7 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Getsuan said to his students: "Keichu, the first wheel-maker of China, made two wheels of fifty spokes each. Now, suppose you removed the nave uniting the spokes. What would become of the wheel? And had Keichu done this, could he be called the master wheel-maker?"

author: Getsuan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 8 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A monk asked Seijo: "I understand that a Buddha who lived before recorded history sat in meditation for ten cycles of existence and could not realize the highest truth, and so could not become fully emancipated. Why was this so?"

Seijo replied: "Your question is self-explanatory."

The monk asked: "Since the Buddha was meditating, why could he not fulfill Buddhahood?"

Seijo said: "He was not a Buddha."

author: Seijo
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 9 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A monk named Seizei asked of Sozan: "Seizei is alone and poor. Will you give him support?"

Sozan asked: "Seizei?"

Seizei responded: "Yes, sir."

Sozan said: "You have Zen, the best wine in China, and already have finished three cups, and still you are saying that they did not even wet your lips."

author: Seizei
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 10 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Joshu Examines a Monk in Meditation

text.en:
Joshu went to a place where a monk had retired to meditate and asked him: "What is, is what?"

The monk raised his fist.

Joshu replied: "Ships cannot remain where the water is too shallow." And he left.

A few days later Joshu went again to visit the monk and asked the same question.

The monk answered the same way.

Joshu said: "Well given, well taken, well killed, well saved." And he bowed to the monk.

author: Joshu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 11 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Zuigan called out to himself every day: "Master."

Then he answered himself: "Yes, sir."

And after that he added: "Become sober."

Again he answered: "Yes, sir."

"And after that," he continued, "do not be deceived by others."

"Yes, sir; yes, sir," he answered.

author: Zuigan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 12 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Tokusan went to the dining room from the meditation hall holding his bowl. Seppo was on duty cooking. When he met Tokusan he said: "The dinner drum is not yet beaten. Where are you going with your bowl?"

So Tokusan returned to his room.

Seppo told Ganto about this. Ganto said: "Old Tokusan did not understand ultimate truth."

Tokusan heard of this remark and asked Ganto to come to him. "I have heard," he said, "you are not approving my Zen." Ganto admitted this indirectly. Tokusan said nothing.

The next day Tokusan delivered an entirely different kind of lecture to the monks. Ganto laughed and clapped his hands, saying: "I see our old man understands ultimate truth indeed. None in China can surpass him."

author: Tokusan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 13 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Nansen Cuts the Cat in Two

text.en:
Nansen saw the monks of the eastern and western halls fighting over a cat. He seized the cat and told the monks: "If any of you say a good word, you can save the cat."

No one answered. So Nansen boldly cut the cat in two pieces.

That evening Joshu returned and Nansen told him about this. Joshu removed his sandals and, placing them on his head, walked out.

Nansen said: "If you had been there, you could have saved the cat."

author: Joshu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 14 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Tozan went to Ummon. Ummon asked him where he had come from.

Tozan said: "From Sato village." 

Ummon asked: "In what temple did you remain for the summer?"

Tozan replied: "The temple of Hoji, south of the lake."

"When did you leave there?" asked Ummon, wondering how long Tozan would continue with such factual answers.

"The twenty-fifth of August," answered Tozan.

Ummon said: "I should give you three blows with a stick, but today I forgive you."

The next day Tozan bowed to Ummon and asked: "Yesterday you forgave me three blows. I do not know why you thought me wrong."

Ummon, rebuking Tozan's spiritless responses, said: "You are good for nothing. You simply wander from one monastery to another."

Before Ummon's words were ended Tozan was enlightened.

author: Tozan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 15 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Ummon asked: "The world is such a wide world, why do you answer a bell and don ceremonial robes?"

author: Ummon
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 16 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: The Three Calls of the Emperor's Teacher

text.en:
Chu, called Kokushi, the teacher of the emperor, called to his attendant: "Oshin." 

Oshin answered: "Yes."

Chu repeated, to test his pupil: "Oshin."

Oshin repeated: "Yes."

Chu called: "Oshin."

Oshin answered: "Yes."

Chu said: "I ought to apologize to you for all this calling, but really you ought to apologize to me."

author: Chu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 17 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A monk asked Tozan when he was weighing some flax: "What is Buddha?" 

Tozan said: "This flax weighs three pounds."

author: Tozan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 18 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Joshu asked Nansen: "What is the path?"

Nansen said: "Everyday life is the path."

Joshu asked: "Can it be studied?"

Nansen said: "If you try to study, you will be far away from it."

Joshu asked: "If I do not study, how can I know it is the path?"

Nansen said: "The path does not belong to the perception world, neither does it belong to the nonperception world. Cognition is a delusion and noncognition is senseless. If you want to reach the true path beyond doubt, place yourself in the same freedom as sky. You name it neither good nor not-good."

At these words Joshu was enlightened.

author: Joshu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 19 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Shogen asked: "Why does the enlightened man not stand on his feet and explain himself?" And he also said: "It is not necessary for speech to come from the tongue."

author: Shogen
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 20 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A monk asked Ummon: "What is Buddha?"

Ummon answered him: "Dried dung."

author: Ummon
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 21 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Ananda asked Kashapa: "Buddha gave you the golden-woven robe of successorship. What else did he give you?"

Kashapa said: "Ananda."

Ananda answered: "Yes, brother."

Said Kashapa: "Now you can take down my preaching sign and put up your own."

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 22 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Do Not Think Good, Do Not Think Not-Good

text.en:
When he became emancipated the sixth patriarch received from the fifth patriarch the bowl and robe given from the Buddha to his successors, generation after generation.

A monk named E-myo out of envy pursued the patriarch to take this great treasure away from him. The sixth patriarch placed the bowl and robe on a stone in the road and told E-myo: "These objects just symbolize the faith. There is no use fighting over them. If you desire to take them, take them now."

When E-myo went to move the bowl and robe they were as heavy as mountains. He could not budge them. Trembling for shame he said: "I came wanting the teaching, not the material treasures. Please teach me."

The sixth patriarch said: "When you do not think good and when you do not think not-good, what is your true self?"

At these words E-myo was illumined. Perspiration broke out all over his body. He cried and bowed, saying: "You have given me the secret words and meanings. Is there yet a deeper part of the teaching?"

The sixth patriarch replied: "What I have told you is no secret at all. When you realize your own true self the secret belongs to you."

E-myo said: "I was under the fifth patriarch many years but could not realize my true self until now. Through your teaching I find the source. A person drinks water and knows himself whether  it is cold or warm. May I call you my teacher?"

The sixth patriarch replied: "We studied together under the fifth patriarch. Call him your teacher, but just treasure what you have attained."

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 23 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A monk asked Fuketsu: "Without speaking, without silence, how can you express the truth?"

Fuketsu observed: "I always remember springtime in southern China. The birds sing among innumerable kinds of fragrant flowers."

author: Fuketsu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 24 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
In a dream Kyozan went to Maitreya's Pure Land. He recognized himself seated in the third seat in the abode of Maitreya. Someone announced: "Today the one who sits in the third seat will preach."

Kyozan arose and, hitting the gavel, said: "The truth of Mahayana teaching is transcendent, above words and thought. Do you understand?"

author: Kyozan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 25 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Two Monks Roll Up the Screen

text.en:
Hogen of Seiryo monastery was about to lecture before dinner when he noticed that the bamboo screen lowered for meditation had not been  rolled up. He pointed to it. Two monks arose from the audience and rolled it up.

Hogen, observing the physical moment, said: "The state of the first monk is good, not that of the other."

author: Mumon Ekai
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 26 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: It Is Not Mind, It Is Not Buddha, It Is Not Things

text.en:
A monk asked Nansen: "Is there a teaching no master ever preached before?"

Nansen said: "Yes, there is."

"What is it?" asked the monk.

Nansen replied: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not things."

author: Nansen
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 27 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Tokusan was studying Zen under Ryutan. One night he came to Ryutan and asked many questions. The teacher said: "The night is getting old. Why don't you retire?"

So Tokusan bowed and opened the screen to go out, observing: "It is very dark outside."

Ryutan offered Tokusan a lighted candle to find his way. Just as Tokusan received it, Ryutan blew it out. At that moment the mind of Tokusan was opened.

"What have you attained?" asked Ryutan. "From now on," said Tokusan, "I will not doubt the teacher's words."

The next day Ryutan told the monks at his lecture: "I see one monk among you. His teeth are like the sword tree, his mouth is like the blood bowl. If you hit him hard with a big stick, he will not even so much as look back at you. Someday he will mount the highest peak and carry my teaching there."

On that day, in front of the lecture hall, Tokusan burned to ashes his commentaries on the sutras. He said: "However abstruse the teachings are, in comparison with this enlightenment they are like a single hair to the great sky. However profound the complicated knowledge of the world, compared to this enlightenment it is like one drop of water to the great ocean." Then he left that monastery.

author: Tokusan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 28 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Not the Wind, Not the Flag

text.en:
Two monks were arguing about a flag. One said: "The flag is moving."

The other said: "The wind is moving."

The sixth patriarch happened to be passing by. He told them: "Not the wind, not the flag; mind is moving."

author: Mumon Ekai
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 29 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Daibai asked Baso: "What is Buddha?"

Baso said: "This mind is Buddha."

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 30 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A traveling monk asked an old woman the road to Taizan, a popular temple supposed to give wisdom to the one who worships there. The old woman said: "Go straight ahead." When the monk proceeded a few steps, she said to herself: "He also is a common church-goer."

Someone told this incident to Joshu, who said: "Wait until I investigate." The next day he went and asked the same question, and the old woman gave the same answer.

Joshu remarked: "I have investigated that old woman."

author: Joshu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 31 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A philosopher asked Buddha: "Without words, without the wordless, will you tell me truth?"

The Buddha kept silence.

The philosopher bowed and thanked the Buddha, saying: "With your loving kindness I have cleared away my delusions and entered the true path."

After the philosopher had gone, Ananda asked the Buddha what he had attained.

The Buddha replied: "A good horse runs even at the shadow of the whip."

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 32 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A monk asked Baso: "What is Buddha?"

Baso said: "This mind is not Buddha."

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 33 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Nansen said: "Mind is not Buddha. Learning is not the path."

author: Nansen
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 34 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: "Seijo, the Chinese girl," observed Goso, "had two souls, one always sick at home and the other in the city, a married woman with two children. Which was the true soul?"

author: Seijo
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 35 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Meeting a Zen Master on the Road

text.en: Goso said: "When you meet a Zen master on the road you cannot talk to him, you cannot face him with silence. What are you going to do?"

author: Goso
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 36 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: A Buffalo Passes Through the Enclosure

text.en: Goso said: "When a buffalo goes out of his enclosure to the edge of the abyss, his horns and his head and his hoofs all pass through, but why can't the tail also pass?"

author: Goso
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 37 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: An Oak Tree in the Garden

text.en:
A monk asked Joshu why Bodhidharma came to China. 

Joshu said: "An oak tree in the garden."

author: Joshu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 38 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A Zen student told Ummon: "Brilliancy of Buddha illuminates the whole universe."

Before he finished the phrase Ummon asked: "You are reciting another's poem, are you not?"

"Yes," answered the student.

"You are sidetracked," said Ummon.

Afterwards another teacher, Shishin, asked his pupils: "At what point did that student go off the track?"

author: Ummon
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 39 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Hyakujo wished to send a monk to open a new monastery. He told his pupils that whoever answered a question most ably would be appointed. Placing a water vase on the ground, he asked: "Who can say what this is without calling its name?"

The chief monk said: "No one can call it a wooden shoe."

Isan, the cooking monk, tipped over the vase with his foot and went out.

Hyakujo smiled and said: "The chief monk loses." And Isan became the master of the new monastery.

author: Hyakujo
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 40 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Bodhidharma sits facing the wall. His future successor stands in the snow and presents his severed  arm to Bodhidharma. He cries: "My mind is not pacified. Master, pacify my mind."

Bodhidharma says: "If you bring me that mind, I will pacify it for you."

The successor says: "When I search my mind I cannot hold it."

Bodhidharma says: "Then your mind is pacified already."

author: Bodhidharma
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 41 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: The Girl Comes Out from Meditation

text.en:
In the time of Buddha Shakyamuni, Manjusri went to the assemblage of the Buddhas. When he arrived there, the conference was over and each Buddha had returned to his own Buddha-land. Only one girl was yet unmoved in deep meditation.

Manjusri asked Buddha Shakyamuni how it was possible for this girl to reach this state, one which even he could not attain. "Bring her out  from Samadhi and ask her yourself," said the Buddha.

Manjusri walked around the girl three times and snapped his fingers. She still remained in meditation. So by his miracle power he transported her to a high heaven and tried his best to call her, but in vain.

Buddha Shakyamuni said: "Even a hundred thousand Manjusris could not disturb her, but below this place, past twelve hundred million countries, is a Bodhisattva, Mo-myo, seed of delusion. If he comes here, she will awaken."

No sooner had the Buddha spoken than that Bodhisattva sprang up from the earth and bowed and paid homage to the Buddha. Buddha directed him to arouse the girl. The Bodhisattva went in front of the girl and snapped his fingers, and in that instant the girl came out from her deep meditation.

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 42 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Shuzan held out his short staff and said: "If you call this a short staff, you oppose its reality. If you do not call it a short staff, you ignore the fact. Now what do you wish to call this?"

author: Shuzan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 43 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Basho said to his disciple: "When you have a staff, I will give it to you. If you have no staff, I will take it away from you."

author: Basho
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 44 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Hoen said: "The past and future Buddhas, both are his servants. Who is he?"

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 45 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Proceed from the Top of the Pole

text.en: Sekiso asked: "How can you proceed on from the top of a hundred-foot pole?" Another Zen teacher said: "One who sits on the top of a hundred-foot pole has attained a certain height but still is not handling Zen freely. He should proceed on from there and appear with his whole body in the ten parts of the world."

author: Sekiso
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 46 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Tosotsu built three barriers and made the monks pass through them. The first barrier is studying Zen. In studying Zen the aim is to see one's own true nature. Now where is your true nature?

Secondly, when one realizes his own true nature he will be free from birth and death. Now when you shut the light from your eyes and become a corpse, how can you free yourself?

Thirdly, if you free yourself from birth and death, you should know where you are. Now your body separates into the four elements. Where are you?

author: Tosotsu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 47 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A Zen pupil asked Kembo: "All Buddhas of the ten parts of the universe enter the one road of Nirvana. Where does that road begin?"

Kembo, raising his walking stick and drawing the figure one in the air, said: "Here it is."

This pupil went to Ummon and asked the same question. Ummon, who happened to have a fan in his hand, said: "This fan will reach to the thirty-third heaven and hit the nose of the presiding deity there. It is like the Dragon Carp of the Eastern Sea tipping over the rain-cloud with his tail."

author: Ummon
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 48 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Amban, a layman Zen student, said: "Mu-mon has just published forty-eight koans and called the book Gateless Gate. He criticizes the old patriarchs' words and actions. I think he is very mischievous. He is like an old doughnut seller trying to catch a passerby to force his doughnuts down his mouth. The customer can neither swallow nor spit out the doughnuts, and this causes suffering. Mu-mon has annoyed everyone enough, so I think I shall add one more as a bargain. I wonder if he himself can eat this bargain. If he can, and digest it well, it will be fine, but if not, we will have to put it back into the frying pan with his forty-eight also and cook them again. Mu-mon, you eat first, before someone else does:

"Buddha, according to a sutra, once said: 'Stop, stop. Do not speak. The ultimate truth is not even to think.'"

 

Amban's comment: Where did that so-called teaching come from? How is it that one could not even think it? Suppose someone spoke about it then what became of it? Buddha himself was a great chatterbox and in this sutra spoke contrarily. Because of this, persons like Mu-mon appear afterwards in China and make useless doughnuts, annoying people. What shall we do after all? I will show you.

Then Amban put his palms together, folded  his hands, and said: "Stop, stop. Do not speak. The ultimate truth is not even to think. And now I will make a little circle on the sutra with my finger and add that five thousand other sutras and Vimalakirti's gateless gate all are here!"

If anyone tells you fire is light,
 Pay no attention.
 When two thieves meet they need no introduction:
 They recognize each other without question.

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 49 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Finding a Diamond on a Muddy Road

text.en: Gudo was the emperor's teacher of Zen. Nevertheless, he used to travel alone as a wandering pilgrim. When he was at the seaside in Edo, some distance from the inn where he was staying, he noticed a tea shop. A girl was working there. "I must buy some tea," thought Gudo, and he called to the girl to bring him a cup. "I'll bring it to you," said the girl, and she brought him a cup of tea. When Gudo held out his hand for the cup, she suddenly poured the tea over his hand. The hot water burned his hand and he nearly dropped the cup. The girl laughed. Startled and angry, Gudo looked at her. "You look like a Zen man," said the girl, "but you don't seem to understand how a person like me fools you. Tell me, now, what is the Buddha?" Gudo tried to answer, but could not. The girl laughed again and went into the shop. Gudo was humiliated. He felt he could not remain in that region. He went to a master and became a serious student at last. After many years he returned home, realizing that he had found a diamond on a muddy road.

author: Gudo
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Zen Master Hakuin was praised by his neighbours as one living a pure life. A beautiful Japanese girl whose parents owned a food store lived near him. Suddenly, without any warning, her parents discovered she was with child. The parents were angry. The girl would not confess who the man was, but after much harassment at last named Hakuin. In great anger the parents went to the master. "Is that so?" was all he would say. After the child was born it was brought to Hakuin. He had lost his reputation, but did not seem to mind. He took very good care of the child. He obtained milk from his neighbours and everything else the little one needed. A year later the girl could stand it no longer. She told her parents the truth — the real father was a young man who worked in the fish market. The parents of the girl at once went to Hakuin, asked his forgiveness, and told him they wanted the child back. Hakuin willingly returned the child. "Is that so?" was all he said.

author: Hakuin
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: The Zen master Ho-Shin was about to die. "Is there any last poem?" asked his students. "I have no poem to write," said Ho-Shin. "I only have a few words: Do not kill. Do not steal. Do not be lustful. Do not lie. Do not take wine." "But master," said one student, "anyone can keep those precepts. What is the special teaching of Zen?" "I have no wish to deceive anyone," replied Ho-Shin. "I just keep the precepts. That is the fundamental teaching of all Buddhas and patriarchs. This is indeed the Zen teaching." "Is that all? That is too simple," said the student. "The truth is not complicated," replied Ho-Shin, and passed away.

author: Ho-Shin
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Shun-Kai was the wife of a merchant. She was beautiful, but proud and willful. When her husband died, her relatives tried to persuade her to remarry, but she refused. She intended to become a nun and study Zen. She went to a Zen master and asked him to ordain her. The master looked at her. "You are too beautiful to become a nun," he said. "You will only bring trouble to the monastery." Shun-Kai went home. That night she heated a pot of oil, and when it was boiling she threw it over her face. In the morning she went back to the master. "Now will you ordain me?" she asked. The master looked at her scarred face. "What determination!" he said. "I will ordain you." After her ordination Shun-Kai became a devoted nun. She attained enlightenment and wrote many beautiful poems about the moon.

author: Shun-Kai
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Anyone who has visited China knows that the Chinese people are always smiling. They smile at you when you meet them on the road. They smile at you in the teahouse. They smile at you on the bus. This is not because they have anything special to be happy about. They smile because they have discovered the secret of happiness. The secret is this: Do not expect anything from anyone. Expect nothing, and you will never be disappointed. When you stop expecting, you begin to live in the present moment. And the present moment is the only moment there is. That is why the Chinese are happy.

author: Chinese saying
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: In Tokyo in the Meiji era there lived two prominent teachers of opposite characteristics. One was Unsho, an instructor in Shingon. He kept Buddha's precepts scrupulously. He never drank intoxicants, nor did he eat after eleven o'clock in the morning. The other was Tanzan, a professor of philosophy at the Imperial University. He never observed the precepts. When he ate he ate without restraint, and when he slept he slept without restraint. Unsho was considered a saint by the people. One day Unsho visited Tanzan, who was drinking wine, not even a drop of which is supposed to touch a Buddhist's tongue. "Hello, brother," Tanzan greeted him. "Won't you have a drink?" "I never drink!" exclaimed Unsho solemnly. "One who does not drink is not even human," said Tanzan. "Do you mean to say I am not human just because I do not drink intoxicants?" Unsho exclaimed in anger. "Then if I am not human, what am I?" "A Buddha," answered Tanzan.

author: Tanzan
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Sho-Un became a teacher of Zen. When he was still a student, his mother used to urge him to study harder. She was a very strict mother who wanted him to become a great Zen master. One day Sho-Un was visiting a distant temple. His mother, who was old and ill, wrote him a letter: "I am very ill. Come home at once." When Sho-Un received the letter he did not go home. Instead he wrote back: "I am sorry I cannot come. I am at a very important stage in my training. If I come home now I will lose all my progress. Please understand." When his mother received this letter, she became very angry. She wrote back: "You are a selfish and unfilial son. If you do not come home I will die cursing you." Still Sho-Un did not go home. He continued his Zen training. When at last he attained enlightenment, he returned home. His mother was still alive. She greeted him with tears and said: "Now I know you are a true Zen master. Forgive my anger. I was a foolish old woman."

author: Sho-Un
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A university student visited a Zen master and asked: "Have you ever read the Bible?" "No," answered the master, "tell me about it." The student opened the Bible and read from the Sermon on the Mount: "And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." The Zen master listened quietly. "Excellent!" he exclaimed when the student had finished. "These words are not far from Buddhahood. Whoever uttered them is an enlightened being."

author: University student
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master named Gettan lived in the northern part of Japan. A young student came to him and asked: "Will you teach me Zen?" "I will," said Gettan, "if you can tell me what Zen is." The student was silent. "Think it over," said Gettan, "and come back when you know." The student went away and thought. He returned the next day. "Zen is the teaching of the Buddha," he said. "That is not it," said Gettan. The student went away again and thought some more. He came back a week later. "Zen is emptiness," he said. "That is not it either," said Gettan. The student went away discouraged. He returned many times with different answers but each time Gettan said no. Finally the student gave up. "Master," he said, "I have no answer. I am a fool." "Now you are ready to learn," said Gettan. "When you know nothing, you can learn everything. I will teach you Zen."

author: Gettan
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Jiun, a Shingon master, was the son of a Buddhist priest. When his mother was about to die, she asked him: "Will you promise me something?" "Anything, mother," said Jiun. "I want you to promise me that you will never become a Zen master," she said. "Why not?" asked Jiun. "Because I have seen too many Zen masters," she said. "They are proud and arrogant. They think they have special knowledge. They look down on ordinary people. Promise me you will be humble." Jiun promised. He became a great Shingon master. He never sat in the Zen meditation posture. He never used Zen words. But he was a Zen master just the same. When anyone asked him about Zen he would say: "I am not a Zen master. I know nothing about Zen." And he would bow and walk away.

author: Jiun
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Mokusen Hiki was living in a temple in the province of Tamba. One of his followers complained of the stinginess of his wife. Mokusen visited the wife and showed her his clenched fist. "What do you mean by that?" asked the surprised woman. "Suppose my fist were always like that," said Mokusen. "What would you call it?" "Deformed," replied the woman. Then he opened his hand flat in her face and asked: "Suppose it were always like that. What then?" "Another kind of deformity," said the wife. "If you understand that much," said Mokusen, "you are a good wife." He left. After his meal Mokusen returned. "I have a poem for you," he said. "Open your hand and give. Close your hand and keep. Both are deformities. The sage gives and keeps. Neither hand nor mind is tight." And he smiled.

author: Mokusen Hiki
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Gi-Sho was a nun who studied Zen with Bankei. She attained enlightenment after many years of practice. When Bankei confirmed her realization, he said: 'Now you understand. You must go out and teach others.' Gi-Sho shook her head. 'I don't want to teach,' she said. 'I just want to meditate in peace.' Bankei laughed. 'You think Zen is just sitting?' he said. 'Zen is life. Every moment is Zen. Every action is Zen. Go and work in the world.' Gi-Sho understood. She went to a poor village and started a school for girls. She taught them to read and write. She taught them to meditate. She lived there for many years, helping the poor. When she died the whole village mourned.

author: Gi-Sho
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young monk asked his teacher: 'Master, I had a dream last night. In the dream I was a butterfly. I flew from flower to flower. I was happy. But when I woke up I was a monk again. Which is real - the monk or the butterfly?' The master laughed. 'When you dream,' he said, 'you are the butterfly. When you wake, you are the monk. Both are real and neither is real. The truth is beyond both.' The monk was puzzled. 'But what is the truth?' he asked. The master said: 'The truth is that you are asking questions while I am trying to sleep. Good night.' And he closed his eyes.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A monk asked Joshu: 'What is Zen?' Joshu said: 'Have you eaten your rice?' 'Yes,' said the monk. 'Then wash your bowl.' At that moment the monk was enlightened. Later another monk asked Joshu: 'What is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West?' Joshu said: 'The oak tree in the garden.' The monk was puzzled. A third monk asked: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature?' Joshu said: 'Mu!' This is the most famous koan in all of Zen. Joshu's Zen is simple and direct. It points to the truth of everyday life.

author: Joshu
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Tosui was a Zen master who lived as a beggar. He wandered from village to village with only a bowl. He never preached. He never taught. He just begged for food and slept in the fields. One day a wealthy merchant recognized him. 'Master Tosui!' he exclaimed. 'Why do you live like this? You are a great Zen teacher. You could have a temple. You could have disciples.' Tosui held out his bowl. 'I have everything I need,' he said. 'I have food when I am hungry. I have a place to sleep when I am tired. I have the sky for my roof and the earth for my bed. What more could I want?' The merchant was silent. 'You are richer than I am,' he said at last. 'I own many things but I am never satisfied. You own nothing and you are content.' Tosui smiled and walked on.

author: Tosui
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

title.en: How Grass and Trees Become Enlightened

text.en: A monk asked his master: 'Do grass and trees also attain enlightenment?' The master said: 'If you say they do, you are wrong. If you say they do not, you are also wrong.' The monk was puzzled. 'What should I say then?' he asked. The master replied: 'Just ask the grass and trees themselves.' The monk went outside and asked a pine tree: 'Do you attain enlightenment?' The pine tree did not answer. The monk returned to the master. 'The pine tree did not answer me,' he said. 'Did you expect it to speak?' asked the master. 'The pine tree has been enlightened from the beginning. It does not need to speak. It does not need to attain anything. It just stands there, being a pine tree. That is its enlightenment.'

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was painting a picture of a bamboo grove. He worked on it for many days. When he finished, he showed it to his students. 'What do you think?' he asked. 'It is beautiful,' they said, 'but the proportions seem wrong. The bamboo is too tall and the leaves are too small.' The master laughed. 'You are looking at it from the outside,' he said. 'If you want to see the true proportions, you must become the bamboo.' He took a brush and painted another picture. This time the bamboo was even taller and the leaves even smaller. 'Now,' said the master, 'this is accurate proportion. When you become the bamboo, you see it as it really is.'

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young monk complained to his master: 'The miso soup is sour today.' The master said nothing. The next day the monk complained again: 'The miso soup is still sour.' Still the master said nothing. The third day the monk said: 'Master, the miso has been sour for three days. Should we throw it away?' The master finally spoke: 'The miso is not sour. Your mind is sour. When your mind is sour, everything tastes sour. When your mind is sweet, everything tastes sweet.' The monk felt ashamed. He stopped complaining. From then on, he tried to keep his mind sweet.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A student came to his master and said: 'I have been practicing Zen for five years and I have made no progress. I feel like giving up.' The master said: 'Have you ever seen a candle that has burned all night? In the morning, just before dawn, the flame flickers. It seems as if it will go out. But if you keep the wick trimmed, if you keep the wax fresh, the candle will burn until the sun rises. Your practice is like that. The darkest hour is just before dawn. Don't give up now. Your light may flicker, but it will not go out. Keep going. The dawn is near.' The student took heart and continued his practice. Soon after, he attained enlightenment.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was dying. His students gathered around him. 'Master,' they said, 'leave us your last teaching.' The master opened his eyes. 'I have nothing to leave you,' he said. 'I have taught you everything I know. Now you must walk your own path.' 'But master,' they insisted, 'at least leave us a poem.' The master smiled weakly. 'My whole life has been my poem,' he said. 'Every breath, every step, every word. If you have understood my life, you have my last teaching. If you have not, no poem will help you.' He closed his eyes. A moment later he opened them again. 'Oh, one more thing,' he said. 'Don't forget to water the garden.' Then he died.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

title.en: The Tea Master and the Assassin

text.en: A tea master was challenged by a samurai who wanted to kill him. The tea master was not a fighter. He was afraid. He went to a Zen master and asked for advice. The Zen master said: 'You are a tea master. When you prepare tea, you are fully present. Your mind is calm. Your movements are precise. Face the samurai with the same mind you have when you make tea.' The tea master understood. He went to meet the samurai. He bowed. He took out his tea utensils. He began to prepare tea with complete concentration. His movements were graceful and precise. The samurai watched in amazement. He had never seen such presence of mind. When the tea master finished, he offered the samurai a cup. The samurai took it and drank. Then he bowed deeply and left. He could not kill a man with such a calm and centered mind.

author: Tea master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young monk asked his master: 'Master, which is the true path to enlightenment? Should I meditate in the mountains? Should I study the sutras? Should I serve the poor?' The master said: 'The true path is right where you are.' 'But I don't understand,' said the monk. 'I am here in the monastery. Is this the true path?' 'The true path,' said the master, 'is washing your bowl after eating. It is sweeping the floor. It is greeting your brothers. It is sitting in meditation. It is all of these and none of these. The true path is not a destination. It is the way you walk. Walk with full attention, and every step is the true path.'

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A soldier came to Hakuin and asked: 'Master, is there really a paradise and a hell?' Hakuin looked at the soldier with contempt. 'Who are you?' he asked. 'I am a samurai,' the soldier replied proudly. 'You, a samurai?' Hakuin laughed. 'You look more like a beggar to me.' The soldier became angry. He drew his sword. Hakuin said calmly: 'Here open the gates of hell.' The soldier understood. He sheathed his sword and bowed. 'And here,' said Hakuin, 'open the gates of paradise.'

author: Hakuin
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A merchant came to a Zen master and said: 'Someone has been stealing from my shop. I suspect a monk from the nearby temple. What should I do?' The master said: 'Arrest the stone Buddha in the garden.' 'Why?' asked the merchant. 'Because the stone Buddha sees everything,' said the master. 'If you arrest the Buddha, he will tell you who stole.' The merchant arrested the stone Buddha and brought it to the magistrate. The magistrate laughed. 'Why have you brought a stone Buddha to court?' 'Because he saw the thief,' said the merchant. The magistrate understood. He said: 'The stone Buddha is innocent. The true thief is your own suspicion. Go home and forgive whoever stole from you.' The merchant went home. The next day, the stolen goods were returned anonymously.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was asked about war and peace. He said: 'The greatest battle is not fought with swords. It is fought in the heart. The enemy is not another person. The enemy is your own ignorance, your own anger, your own greed. Conquer these, and you have conquered all enemies. True warriors are not those who kill others. True warriors are those who kill their own delusions. They are soldiers of humanity, fighting the war against suffering.' The student asked: 'But what about those who wage real war?' The master replied: 'They have not yet learned to fight the only battle that matters. Pity them, and teach them peace.'

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young man came to a Zen master and said: 'I am very unhappy. Everything goes wrong in my life. Nothing ever works out for me. I think I am cursed.' The master said: 'Give me your hand.' The young man held out his hand. The master studied his palm. 'I see,' said the master. 'Your lifeline shows you will live to be eighty. Your fortune line shows you will be rich. Your love line shows you will have a happy marriage. But none of this matters.' 'Why not?' asked the young man. 'Because,' said the master, 'the lines in your hand change with every thought, every action, every moment. You are not in the hands of destiny. Destiny is in your hands.'

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was asked how many disciples he had. 'Ten,' he replied. 'But master,' said the student, 'I see only five in the meditation hall.' 'Some of my disciples are not in the hall,' said the master. 'One is a fisherman. One is a farmer. One is a merchant. One is a mother. One is a child.' The student was confused. 'How can they be your disciples if they do not meditate?' he asked. 'They meditate while fishing,' said the master. 'They meditate while farming. They meditate while selling. They meditate while raising children. They meditate while playing. Zen is not only in the meditation hall. It is everywhere. My real disciples are those who bring Zen into everyday life.'

text.en: A monk said to his master: 'I want to become a better person. I want to reform myself. What should I do?' The master asked: 'What do you think is wrong with you?' The monk listed his faults: anger, laziness, greed, pride. The master nodded. 'These are not your faults,' he said. 'These are your teachers. Each one has something to teach you. Instead of fighting them, learn from them.' 'But how?' asked the monk. 'When anger arises,' said the master, 'do not suppress it. Observe it. Where does it come from? Where does it go? When you understand anger, you are free from anger. This is true reformation - not to change yourself, but to understand yourself.'

text.en: A student was meditating when he smelled incense. He opened his eyes and saw his master burning incense. 'Master,' said the student, 'the incense is distracting me. I cannot meditate.' The master took the incense burner and placed it in front of the student. 'Now meditate on the incense,' he said. 'Do not resist it. Become one with it.' The student closed his eyes. He breathed in the scent. He became the scent. He forgot himself. When he opened his eyes, an hour had passed. 'Now you understand,' said the master. 'Zen is not about avoiding distractions. It is about becoming one with everything, including distractions.'

text.en: A master said: 'There are three kinds of disciples. The first kind hears the teaching and immediately understands. The second kind hears the teaching and thinks about it. The third kind hears the teaching and rejects it. All three reach the same destination. It just takes different amounts of effort.' A student asked: 'Which kind am I, master?' The master said: 'The kind that asks questions instead of finding out for himself.'

text.en: A young monk was trying to light a fire. He struck match after match but the wood would not catch. He became frustrated. He struck harder. The matches broke. He threw down the box in anger. The master, who had been watching, picked up a fire poker. He stirred the ashes gently. A small ember glowed beneath the surface. He placed a piece of kindling on it and blew softly. A flame appeared. 'Sometimes,' said the master, 'the fire is already there. You just need to uncover it. Zen is not about creating something new. It is about uncovering what is already there.'

text.en: A monk said: 'Master, I have given up everything. I own nothing. I am free.' The master pointed to the monk's robe. 'You are attached to that robe,' he said. The monk took off his robe. 'Now I have nothing,' he said. 'You are attached to having nothing,' said the master. The monk was silent. 'Non-attachment,' said the master, 'is not about having nothing. It is about being free even when you have everything. It is about holding things lightly, with open hands. A man who clings to poverty is as attached as a man who clings to wealth.'

text.en: A student asked: 'Master, what is the Buddha's Zen?' The master held up a flower. 'Is that all?' asked the student. The master put the flower down. 'No,' he said. 'The flower is just a flower. The Buddha's Zen is not in the flower. It is in the seeing. When you see the flower without any thought, without any judgment, without any name - that is the Buddha's Zen. The flower is just a pointer. The real teaching is wordless.' The student looked at the flower. He tried to see without thinking. After a long silence, he smiled. 'I see,' he said. 'What do you see?' asked the master. 'Just a flower,' said the student.
